procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated March 10, 1964, of the Bombay High Court in Criminal Appeals.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: Accused Nos. 2 and 3 were convicted by the Trial Court. The State Government appealed against the acquittal of accused No. 4. The High Court maintained the conviction and sentences of accused Nos. 2 and 3 and set aside the acquittal of accused No. 4, convicting and sentencing him to rigorous imprisonment.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The convicted accused (presumably accused Nos. 2, 3, and 4) filed appeals in the Supreme Court by special leave.

directions: We reduce their sentence to one year's rigorous imprisonment.
The sentence of fine imposed on them shall stand.
Their bill is cancelled and they shall surrender forthwith.

issue.issue_text: Whether there was sufficient evidence to convict the clerk for the offence of cheating.

facts: The accused was a 'mere clerk' in the R.R. firm and the nephew of the other accused.

The only evidence against him was that he (a) wrote some invoices, none of which were found to be the inflated ones, (b) delivered documents, including the fraudulent ones, to the J.R. firm as a servant of his firm, and (c) drew up some pay-in-slips at the request of the J.R. firm.
There was no evidence to show that the clerk participated in the negotiations with the J.R. firm or that he personally made the inflated invoices and hundies.
Crucially, there was no charge of conspiracy filed against the accused.
law: To be convicted of cheating, there must be good and proper evidence that the accused made a representation to induce the victim to part with their funds.

In the absence of a conspiracy charge, the actions of an individual accused must be evaluated on their own to determine guilt, and evidence of association or actions that might be relevant in a conspiracy case cannot be used to infer guilt for a substantive offense like cheating.
application: The Court found no evidence that the clerk made any representation to the J.R. firm to induce them to provide funds.
There was no proof that the clerk knew the invoices were inflated or that the hundies would not be honored. His actions were viewed as those of a servant following instructions.

The Court reasoned that without a conspiracy charge, his actions as a clerk were 'capable of a different interpretation' (i.e., an innocent one) unless a specific intention to cheat could be proven, of which there was no evidence.
The fact that none of the invoices actually written by the clerk were the fraudulent ones further weakened the case against him.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the evidence against the clerk fell short of the legal requirements to prove the offense of cheating. Since there was no proof of any representation made by him or any intention on his part to cheat, and no conspiracy was charged, he was entitled to an acquittal. The Court, therefore, overturned the High Court's conviction and acquitted him.

issue.issue_text: Whether it is proper for a court to reduce a sentence in exchange for the accused returning the cheated amount to the complainant.

facts: The accused, who were convicted of cheating, offered to pay back the money they had wrongly obtained from the complainant.
This offer was made to the High Court and subsequently to the Supreme Court with the hope of receiving a reduced prison sentence in return.
The High Court had entertained this proposal, even adjourning the appeal to allow the accused to deposit the money.
law: The Court established the principle that offences must be tried and punished according to the guilt of the accused and the specific facts of the case.
Any leniency in sentencing must also be based on the facts of the case, not on a financial arrangement.
application: The Supreme Court described the practice of reducing a sentence in exchange for payment as a "bargain" and stated that it is "very wrong for a court to enter into a bargain of this character."
The Court reasoned that it should not act as an agency to recover money for a complainant.
The Court explicitly disapproved of the "unusual course" taken by the High Court in considering such an offer.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the idea that a sentence could be reduced in exchange for the accused returning the cheated amount. It held that punishment must be based on the accused's guilt and the facts of the case, and a court should never be a party to a bargain that trades a lighter sentence for financial restitution to the complainant.

issue.issue_text: Whether the sentence imposed on the partner and munim should be reduced.

facts: The partner (accused No. 2) and the munim (accused No. 3) were found guilty of cheating the J.R. Firm.
In their appeal to the Supreme Court, they offered to pay back the money they had wrongly obtained from the J.R. Firm in exchange for a reduced sentence.
This was a similar offer to one they had made in the High Court, where they deposited money with the court in the hope of getting a reduced sentence.
law: The Court established the principle that it is "very wrong for a court to enter into a bargain" with an accused person.
Punishment should be determined based on the guilt of the accused and the facts of the case.
A court should not act as an agency to recover money for a complainant in exchange for showing leniency in sentencing.
application: The Supreme Court strongly disapproved of the High Court's willingness to consider reducing the sentence in exchange for payment and refused to adopt a similar course.
It explicitly rejected the suggestion to increase the fine as a way to reduce the prison sentence, viewing it as an improper bargain.

However, the Court did find a different reason for leniency. It considered the fact that the accused's firm had a history of many regular transactions and that the fraud was only exposed because the firm unexpectedly became insolvent.
The Court reasoned that, but for this intervening insolvency, the accused might have been able to pay back the money.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court reduced the sentence for the partner and munim to one year's rigorous imprisonment. It did so not because of their offer to pay back the money (which it condemned as an improper bargain), but because it viewed the firm's sudden insolvency as a mitigating factor that prevented the accused from potentially making good on the payments.

arguments.issue_text: Whether there was sufficient evidence to convict the clerk for the offence of cheating.
appellant_arguments: There was no evidence against the clerk (the fourth accused).
He was a mere clerk and there is nothing to show that he took part in the negotiations or in the making of the inflated invoices and hundies.
There is no evidence that he had an intention to cheat the J.R. Firm.
No representation was made by him to induce the J.R. Firm to part with funds.
There is no proof that he knew the invoices were inflated or that the hundies were not going to be met.
None of the invoices that he personally wrote were found to be inflated.
respondent_arguments: The clerk's actions, such as writing some invoices, taking them to the J.R. Firm, and drawing up pay-in-slips at the firm's instance, were sufficient to prove his guilt in the offence of cheating.

arguments.issue_text: Whether it is proper for a court to reduce a sentence in exchange for the accused returning the cheated amount to the complainant.
appellant_arguments: The court should reduce the sentence of imprisonment because the accused are willing to pay the amount they wrongly realised from the complainant.
The court should increase the fine with a view to reducing the sentence of imprisonment.
respondent_arguments: Offences should be tried and punished according to the guilt of the accused, not based on a bargain.
The court should not act as an agency to recover money for the complainant.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the sentence imposed on the partner and munim should be reduced.
appellant_arguments: The High Court should have reduced the sentence imposed on the partner and the munim.
respondent_arguments: The conviction for a bold attempt to get more money through false documents was proper, and the sentence should be maintained.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A court must not be a party to a bargain where a sentence is reduced in exchange for the accused paying money to the complainant; offences must be tried and punished based on the guilt of the accused and the facts of the case, not on a financial arrangement to recover money for the victim.
obiter: The willingness of an accused to pay back wrongfully obtained money may be a factor in considering leniency, as it might suggest an intent to make restitution if not for supervening circumstances like insolvency.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court acquitted the clerk due to a lack of evidence proving he had knowledge of the fraud or an intention to cheat, finding his actions as a mere clerk were insufficient for a conviction. However, the court upheld the convictions of the partner and munim, concluding they had clearly engineered a plan to cheat by using inflated invoices and false hundies to secure larger loans. While the court strongly rejected the principle of reducing a sentence in exchange for repayment, deeming it an improper bargain, it independently reduced the sentences of the partner and munim based on the mitigating factor that they might have repaid the money had their firm not become insolvent.
legal_tests_applied: To establish the offence of cheating, there must be sufficient evidence to prove an intention to cheat. The actions of an accused must be shown to be more than just the routine duties of a clerk; there must be proof of knowledge that the documents were fraudulent or that a representation was made to induce the victim to part with funds.
why_appellant_lost: The partner and munim's argument for a reduced sentence in exchange for repaying the cheated amount was rejected because the court found it is 'very wrong for a court to enter into a bargain of this character' and that the court 'should never be a party to a bargain by which money is recovered for the complainant through their agency.'

The partner and munim's conviction for cheating was upheld because the court determined they had 'engineered a plan under which a larger sum could be borrowed than what could be if the true facts were known' and that it was a 'bold attempt .to ge.t more money through false documents which were to form security for the loans.'
why_respondent_won: The State's position that the partner and munim were guilty of cheating was accepted, as the court found they devised a method using 'inflated invoices and false hundies' to get larger loans than the actual value of the goods represented.

The State's argument against reducing the sentence as part of a bargain was accepted, with the court affirming the principle that 'Offences should be tried and punished according to the guilt of the accused,' not based on a deal to recover money for the complainant.
policy_considerations: It is very wrong for a court to enter into a bargain of this character. Offences should be tried and punished according to the guilt of the accused.

If the Court thinks that leniency can be shown on the facts of the case it may impose a lighter sentence. But the court should never be a party to a bargain by which money is recovered for the complainant through their agency.
